en: The Story of the Vow of Day and Night.
Oṃ, homage to the Dharmadhātu!
It is pure as space, truly existent, and the locus of qualities free from conceptual proliferation.
Homage to him who is the self of the stūpa, consisting of the five aggregates and peaceful. // 1 //

At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Kapilavastu together with about five hundred bhikṣus, many others who had accomplished their task, whose senses were subdued, whose outflows were exhausted,
as well as hundreds of other bodhisattvas born from the six perfections, endowed with the five eyes, and numerous chief disciples— an unsurpassed field of merit.

Adorned by many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others who had donned [the robes] and delighted in the Buddha’s teaching, and filled with their respective retinues— in that assembly, Subhūti spoke thus to Vajradhara:
"O glorious Vajradhara, tiger among sages, in that assembly where many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others were gathered, why did you not speak with a single voice an authoritative command?"
"What is your desire, Subhūti? Express your intention to Śākyamuni as you wish.
Subhūti said:
"My desire is for the supreme vow among men, which is the day-and-night vow, the king of vows, of great success."
When this had been said, Vajradhara, having respectfully honored the Great One’s approval, spoke thus to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, O tiger among sages, not even a single word has been spoken that is not desired by all those present in the assembly. Subhūti, however, desires the King of Vows, which brings great exaltation; he says, 'I desire the ritual procedure for the day-and-night vow.'"
"O Lord of Munis, please explain all of that.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Vajradhara! For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, you have asked a fruitful question; I shall fulfill it."
Having spoken thus, he remained in the glorious *dharmadhātu-samādhi*;
blazing forth the *dharma-jvala* upon the great lotus at the tip of his nose, he illuminated all directions and shone resplendently within that assembly. // 2 //
Then some people in the entire assembly [thought], "This is a sublime, well-spoken Dharma teaching," while others [longed] to drink the nectar of the Blessed One’s words;
likewise, others conversed with one another, saying, "Excellent!
The rays of the Blessed One have appeared; he will surely proclaim a discourse on the Dharma."
Then Vajradhara spoke again:
"Excellent, Blessed One of Great Radiance! O Blessed One, by whom on this earth was the vow of day and night set in motion? Tell me, O Supreme Lord!
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Vajradhara of great splendor, to the supreme vow among vows, the purifying tale upon this earth.
In ancient times, in the northern region, there was a great city named Dharmapattana, equal to the city of Maghavan and filled with the most excellent of virtuous people.
How was that city laid out?
It is seven yojanas in circumference and wide in extent; it is surrounded by rows of palm trees and moats, and is a place of great festivals.
Above that lies Mount Trikūṭa.

It is filled with various kinds of trees, resounds with the constant songs of various flocks of birds, is scented with the fragrance of various flowers, and is made most fragrant by many ṛṣis—Trikūṭa itself.

The city was crowded with many heroes, filled with many learned men, populated by those skilled in various arts, and abounding in many excellent persons such as preeminent physicians; it was also endowed with ministers who knew the seasons, understood the proper times, were aware of conventions, and possessed discernment.
In that city there was a king named Dharmadakṣa, who was knowledgeable in policy, discipline, discrimination, and ritual procedure.

He was by nature affectionate toward his subjects, compassionate, and one who felt the suffering or happiness of others as his own; he was devoted to the Dharma that protects the Dharma and regarded the affairs of others as his own great festival.
His wife was ever-observant of her vows, always practicing righteousness, and endowed with the virtues of learning.
Now at that time, on that mountain Trikūṭa, there dwelt a great-souled venerable one named Śāriputra, a knower of the Jina and the foremost among those who know the Buddha’s wisdom.
Then Śāriputra reflected:
"Who is there who is fond of the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, and practices the Dharma? Where is such a person?"
At that moment, he remembered and said, "It has been shown to me:
there is a king named Dharmacaraṇa, who is affectionate toward the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, and skilled in the Dharma;
I shall teach him that Dharma."
Having said this, he went to the great city of Dharmapattana and arrived there;
in that place there was a certain palace,
and he stayed within it.
He remained there, teaching the Dharma in many ways; all the people there gave him their approval because of his inspiring demeanor. Thereupon, some virtuous men became his disciples.

Then the Great King Dharmadakṣa, having heard the entire account as it had been approved, with reflection, reverence, and respect, caused him to enter the royal palace with great celebration and established him with lodging and food. Then Śāriputra spoke words of blessing to the king.
"May you practice the True Dharma; may there be well-being! May you practice the True Dharma, my child! May you practice the True Dharma for liberation! May all your desires be fulfilled!
Then, having heard these words of blessing with great joy, the king spoke thus to Śāriputra:
"O Lord Śāriputra, what kind of blessing is this of yours?"
"May some Buddha, or a god, or a goddess, or Maheśvara, or Nārāyaṇa, or someone else grant me the benediction, 'May you protect [me]'!
You, however, give [the benediction], 'Practice the True Dharma!
World-Honored One, I do not know the True Dharma; O Mahāmati, please speak of the True Dharma!"
Śāriputra said:
"O Great King, you do not know the supreme dharma among all phenomena; how indeed can the dharmadhātu be called 'dharma,' that most excellent source of names? (3)
Listen, O King of great splendor! Having first performed the consecration of the *dharmadhātu*, one should observe the day-and-night vow (*ahorātravrata*).

Now, whether in a hermitage, a city, a monastery, or wherever else the *dharmadhātu* exists, there one should perform the day-and-night vow. Day and night—this is the "day-and-night" [period]; that vow is the True Dharma (*saddharma*), as established by the Tathāgatas of old.
The king said:
"O best of monks, please explain the ritual procedures and so forth;
tell me, in due order, about the king of vows, the days, months, and other durations within cyclic existence."
Śāriputra said:
"O Great King, first one should perform the placement of the barley-water and the placement of the four deities, beginning with the Dharmadhātu.
Those beings who so desire—whether they be of the four castes, such as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—should observe the vow of the four castes."
He is joined with others through sixteen or twenty births, each according to their own suitability.
O King, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvinī, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
at midday, one should perform the shaving ritual, a pure bath, and the giving of gifts.
Then, when sixty ghaṭikās of the sun have passed, one should take a meal of śāli rice;
thereafter, the washing of the face... [should be done] afterwards.
At that time, one should listen to the exposition. Then, [one should proceed].
O King, at the third watch of the night, everyone should rise; at the time of dawn, having bathed, performed their ritual duties, and put on clean garments, they should undertake the vow.

Having prepared a maṇḍala of the five deities, smeared it with fresh cow dung, and offered the *argha* water, one should perform the sixteen-fold worship for the stūpa, O King, consisting of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings, lutes, flutes, clay drums, muraja drums, paṭaha drums, cymbals, conchs, banners, parasols, songs, dances, and so forth—filled with various festivals—and first perform five circumambulations.
A hymn of praise is sung to the Buddha;
one should scatter parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers upon the summit of the caitya.
Then the king said:
"O best of monks, O one of great wisdom, should the *ahorātra-vrata* be performed in one place, or in a second, or elsewhere?
Śāriputra replied:
"Not in one place, O Great King, but wherever a *caitya* is established."
In whatever temple or shrine, at whatever confluence of sacred sites, or wherever one may wander in a delightful Buddha-field; (5)
The King asked: "O Lord, what is the measure for the circumambulation of an ascetic’s shrine—should it continue as long as the day lasts, or otherwise? What is its extent?
Śāriputra replied:
"O Great King, for ascetics there is neither sleep, nor rest, nor any running about; such is their measure."
The King said:
"O Lord, tell me the distinction between one who is capable and one who is incapable.
Śāriputra replied:
Some who were either incapable or elderly said, "O Great King, the vow for a day and night should not be undertaken.
The king said, "How so, O monk of great wisdom? How could those who are incapable, the young, and the old be recipients of the Dharma?"
Śāriputra said:
Having observed the fast and performed the worship of the caityas, including bathing and other rites, one should perform recitation and hymns of praise.

Furthermore, for those who are incapable or for children, whenever they desire, having observed the fast for one day, or half a day, or even for a single watch (prahara), they should perform the worship of the caityas and circumambulate them once, twice, or thrice.
"O Great King, one should act according to one's ability.
[The king asked: "O Bhikṣu, what is the observance of the vow? What is the food and drink? Furthermore, how does one fulfill the vow? And what is the conclusion of the vow?"

Śāriputra said: Having performed the ritual bathing and other purifications, one should examine the internal mind with every pure offering, accompanied by fragrant flowers, having laid aside staffs and weapons, having ceased the killing of living beings, having abandoned the taking of what is not given, having renounced lustful conduct, and having cast off slander.

By abandoning divergent speech, by abandoning unseen talk, and by abandoning harsh words; and not by harboring covetousness, nor by a mind of ill-will, nor by the adoption of wrong views; nor indeed by the consumption of salt, nor by the thirst for drinking intoxicants, nor by the eating of meat; [and] without high beds, without the transgression of seniority, and without eating at improper times.
Thus, O Great King, one should perform the ritual according to this very procedure;
one should partake of the food at the end of each day and night.
Furthermore, O Great King, for the sake of fulfilling the vow, one should complete the vow every year, or for one year, or three years, or five, or seven.
During the completion of the vow, one should perform the raising of the variegated parasol and the parasol with various offerings, including the planting of flowers.

One should perform the raising of the banner while providing entertainment through various festivals, dances, songs, laughter, *lāsya* movements, and graceful gestures, while the time is filled with the five musical notes and food is taken at the proper intervals; and while scattering flowers, unbroken rice, flour-cakes, and other items.

Having performed the sacrifice and other rites according to the rules, one should then provide the preceptor (*ācārya*) with garments, food, gold, bracelets, and so forth for the fulfillment [of the vow].
Thus, O Great King, the preceptor should then perform the consecration for the sake of auspiciousness for the initiate by means of the teacher;
thereafter, he should cause the worship of the maiden to be performed.
Such, O Great King, is the ritual procedure.
The king said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! I have heard about the undertaking of the vow.
O Lord, please explain its fruit according to your own understanding. (16)
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the fruit of this king of vows;
that singular teaching on the vow was spoken by the Tathāgatas of old. (7)
The lord of the asuras known as Nirghoṣadamana is celebrated;
having reached Amarāvatī, he dwells there in the play of happiness. (8)
Then Indra, the lord of the gods, dejected and sorrowful, reflected:
"By what means shall I be victorious?
The lord of the asuras, Nairṛtadaamana, remains in my hermitage."
Thinking thus, Śakra, the lord of the gods, went to the great *caitya* established in this Trāyastriṃśa abode for the purpose of worship by former lords of the gods;
in that *caitya*, the lord of the gods performed the day-and-night vow according to the prescribed rite.
Immediately thereafter, Nirghoṣadamana, the lord of the asuras, having been defeated, was cast down to the earth.
"Thus, Great King, such is the power of the vow of a single day and night as I have heard it.
The king said: "How so, Bhikṣu Mahāsattva? What is the fruit of that, and what else?"
And speak that entire king of vows in its full detail.
Śāriputra said:
"Listen, O King of great splendor, as I describe to you in its entirety and correctly the fruit of that vow, from beginning to end."
When mortals erect a high canopy for a Tathāgata or for the Dharmadhātu of Śrī, they forever abandon old age, misfortune, birth ending in death, and all disease. (11)
By establishing the Dharma, the Jewel, the peacock, the lotus, and the four banners, one completes the powers of the Buddhas through the four abodes beginning with loving-kindness. // 12 //
To the Dharmadhātu, at the commencement of the vow, one offers water for the feet (*pādya*) mixed with red sandalwood, milk, and so forth; by that, one obtains a great treasure with a pure body.
Having visualized the sipping of water (*ācamana*) there, it is offered here, whereby the sins of this birth are destroyed.
To the Dharmadhātu... [one] transgresses.
Those people who place milk, unbroken rice, water, the nine jewels, and so forth in a conch shell and offer them to the Dharmadhātu will obtain the fruits of their desires in the realm of Sukhāvatī.

Those who present fine cotton cloths, silken garments, and delicate fabrics to the Dharmadhātu will enjoy celestial garments in the city of the gods for as many lifetimes as there are threads in those cloths.
By the offering of *tilaka* paste, one obtains supreme beauty, physical form, excellent qualities, and great fragrance.

And various flowers... [Avk_P_19] Furthermore, the sages always declare that the fruit of a gift equal to a golden creeper is directed toward the Buddhas in their stūpas or images: for every step taken, one should give a single piece of gold.
The sages have declared that to be its fruit; therefore, one should indeed perform the hymn of praise.

The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is honored by the celestial realms... By him who sings and chants before the stupas and images, having attained divine hearing, the divine sound is heard in the city of the gods. O King, by him who recites even a single mantra in the realm of phenomena, the wisdom of the Sugata is attained and meditative absorption (samādhi) is further acquired. Those various musical instruments that are played, O Great King, remain as echoes of divine music in the world of the gods within the realm of phenomena.

Those who perform dances accompanied by various musical instruments before the *dharmadhātu*, stūpas, or images, shall attain the enjoyment of happiness in the world of the gods and sport together with the *gandharvas*. For one dancing with weapons and missiles in hand, all misdeeds are destroyed by those very weapons.
Those who apply a coating of lime to a shrine or an image, though drenched by a mass of evil, proceed to the world of the gods.

Those who descend upon the four directions from a stūpa image, or who offer garlands of flowers to the directions numbering three hundred and sixty, wrapped in a hundred thousand flowers— by virtue of that number of flower-wrappings, they shall obtain enjoyments in the world of the gods for many births. Those who offer various parasols, or variegated parasols, O Great King, become kings.
Universal monarchs, having conquered through the fourfold army, become wanderers in heaven, having gone to the world of the gods, and they attain the state of the Jinas.
Thus, O Great King, I have briefly described to you the fruit of this king of vows for a day and night.
The King said:
"O best of monks, O one of great supernormal knowledge, [it is said that] one should not sleep; thus one resorts to rest, yet one does not take rest—how can the fruit of that be full of faults?
Śāriputra replied:
"By means of that through which sleep and rest are taken, a tenth part of the fruit is obtained."
Then the king said:
"O Śāriputra, the fruit of this king of vows has thus become deficient. Is there a remedy for this, or not?"
Śāriputra said:
"Great King, there is a method for that.
However, one should first bow to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and then perform an eight-limbed prostration while engaged in five circumambulations."
Having asked for forgiveness, one should entreat [the preceptor] with reverence;
by that, one is released from all faults.
Thus, O Great King, the observance of the day-and-night vow has great benefits and a great fruit.

The sin of killing a Brahmin, the sin of killing a child, the sin of killing a uterine brother or sister, the sin of killing a cow, the sin of killing one's mother, the sin of killing one's father, and the sin of destroying a stūpa—
the full fruit of thousands of such acts is obtained from even a single one of these;
thus it was spoken by the Tathāgatas, and thus have I heard.

Whether it be seven mountains, or a load of earth, or another hundred loads, or a thousand *palas*, or even ten million *palas*—in that same way, I am unable to calculate even a fraction or a portion of the limit of the fruit of this King of Vows for a day and night;
such, O Great King, is the immeasurable fruit of the King of Vows. What need is there to mention anything else?
In this way, O Great King, one who is skilled in the Dharma and has attained the full fruit of the teachings should give one-seventh of the dharmas to the sovereign;
one part to the charioteers and the elephant-keepers; and another one part to the inhabitants of the land and those observing vows.
Such, O Great King, is the measure of the portions.
The king said:

"Excellent! O Greatly Wise One, this is indeed the truth: it is the supreme vow among vows, renowned as the King of Vows. O Greatly Intelligent One, my desire was that I would perform it perfectly; this is my firm resolve."
At that very moment, the king summoned his queen, who was observing a vow, and gave her instructions.

Having assembled all the ministers, attendants, and others—numbering ten or twenty people—he had a great caitya constructed. Following the instructions given by Śāriputra, he prepared all the necessary materials and rituals and stood ready.
Then he dispatched messengers;
at that time, the footprints and other items that had arrived from the beginning were installed.
On the fourteenth day, having observed a fast, an offering of lamps was presented to the Dharmadhātu at midday.
Then, having performed the rinsing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, the complete exposition by Śāriputra is heard.
Thereafter, rising at the third watch of the day and night, and having performed the bath and other rites at dawn, the vow is undertaken.

Then, during the course of the vow, one proceeds to the *dharmadhātu*—whether at a *caitya*, a temple, a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or a vast buddha-field—filled with the performance of five circumambulations and so forth, the scattering of parched grain and unbroken rice, and the celebration of various festivals accompanied by hymns and songs.
He proceeded without seeking sleep or rest. At night, many lamps were lit;
setting ablaze garlands of lamps before each shrine and deity, he performed various dances, songs, laughter, and rhythmic movements, traversing [the path] day and night.

O Vajradhara, just as it was instructed by Śāriputra, having fulfilled the three-year period according to this rite, they ascend the various [structures] beginning with the garland of directions and ending with the parasol.
Then, having performed the worship of the maidens (kumāripūjā), the release from the vow is performed.
Thus, O Vajradhara, the great king Dharmadakṣa performed the King of Vows for one day and night.

Then, with great reverence, the Great King Dharmadakṣa gave to Śāriputra a pearl necklace worth a thousand [pieces of gold], as well as various ornaments and everything down to the monastery grounds and robes.
Thereafter, the king composed this verse of supplication:
"Forgive me, O Great Being, in this great success of the King of Vows!"
"By the grace of your feet, my share has not yet been obtained. // 14 //
Śāriputra, having become [thus], spoke again:
"O Great King, listen to my words alone according to your fortune; I shall proclaim for you the sūtra that accords with the past and the ritual procedure. (15)
In one place, O Great King, there was a certain shrine belonging to a penance grove created by the Bodhisattva named Mahāmati; furthermore,
there was a lake named Mahātavī where a male and female nāga resided.

That shrine-hermitage became exceedingly beautiful, covered and filled with various kinds of flowers. At that shrine, five sages worshipped daily with devotion through various recitations, chants, and austerities. One day, a male and female naga bit one of those sages there; then, experiencing the pain of the snake's bite, the sage uttered a curse.
"Why have you two, the Naga and the Nagini, bitten me while I was armored?
May you both be destroyed in seven pieces!
Then, by the mere utterance of that curse, the Naga and the Nagini became seven *śambuka* shells in another birth.

While they were wandering in this manner, Śambukā and Nāgajanmā constantly beheld a shrine (caitya) and came to remember their conduct in a previous birth. Once, having been bitten by a sage devoted to a shrine, I experienced this birth as Śambukā and became distraught.
Thereafter, remembering that a stalk of grain in the field was a shrine, they circumambulated it.

Then, on the fourth day, seven daughters were born to the great king Śambuka, named Kīrakīrti. These daughters were learned in the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*) and lived according to their vows.
While those seven daughters were engaged in ascetic practice (*tapas*), showers of flowers fell constantly.
Having performed these various deeds, they are placed in celestial flower-palaces and led to the world-system of Sukhāvatī.
Śāriputra returned to his own home.
By the power of the King of Vows for Day and Night, Dharmadakṣa, the great king, attained liberation.
The Great Being, dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, possessing sublime radiance, having shattered the full impurity of the Kali age, attained therein incomparable and all-encompassing sovereign bliss.
Whoever causes the Sugata’s sutra, which is their own good fortune, to be heard in accordance with the Dharma,
thereafter the assembly members depart for their respective abodes in the great city of Kapilavastu.
The Blessed One, together with his disciples, remained in meditative absorption.
Thus ends the narrative of the one-day vow (ahorātravrata).
